text_fidelity_a:
HP ENVY Desktop Computer, Intel Core i7-10700, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB Hard Drive & 512 GB SSD Storage, Windows 10 Pro (TE01-1254, 2020 Model) It is an alright system if you are only going to be doing basic computing like Microsoft Office, email, and some Netflix (but maybe not all at the same time). However, at a current price of over $850 being saddle with only the onboard graphics is hardly acceptable. Second, this system is also only okay if you never plan to repair the computer if there are issues with the power supply or motherboard. If you toss out your systems when they break, then this will work. If you like to swap out the bad parts, run for the hills you do not want to be stuck dealing with the HP part store.

If you want to play any games or use programs that require a bit more heavy lifting, (design software, CAD, or anything pulling a bunch of images or rendering) or need to have several programs running at once, you are going to struggle without a graphics card.

But can't you just add your own Graphics Card, I mean it is 2020 after all? Well... while this system does have an open slot on the motherboard for the addition of a graphics card it is severely handicapped in using it. For one, it is a very small case and you will be stuck with a small form factor card, which tend to be more expensive than their standard size counterparts. Worse yet, the included system power is only 180 watts. You cannot run much past whatever is already in the system with that, so you will need to also upgrade the power supply. Here is where it gets annoying. HP not only uses their own motherboard (Baker in this system) but the motherboard uses a proprietary connection to the power supply, so you HAVE TO BUY their power supply and only theirs. There is not an adapter, I looked and looked and looked some more.

That means heading over to the HP parts store website and trying not to pound your head into a wall with how backwards and outdated their system is. If you manage to locate the ONLY 400 watt power supply that works with the baker motherboard (yes 400 watt is the biggest they make that work for this case and motherboard) you will be hit with a $125 price tag (more like $150 after tax and shipping) for a power supply that should really cost half that. Which even if it says is in stock, will likely be back-ordered. They told me I'd be lucky to see it in 2 months even if it says "instock" in the system. Because they are the only ones selling it, you have to either wait or just forget about the upgrade. If you NEED it because your current power supply isn't working, well too bad for you.

If you have hung in this far and managed to get the power supply squared away, you can start on the graphics card piece. Now here is where it gets fun, you will want to avoid the HP parts store. They have the GTX 1660ti listed but its price bounces from over $1000 (yes a grand) to around $700 for a card that is about $300 on Amazon. Due to the power supply limitations a 1660ti is as high as you are going to be able to get, which puts you on par with an entry level gaming laptop. Due to size limitations of the HP Envy case you will want to stick to a small form factor card (generally that means one fan not two, but measure first some of those single fans are still a bit long).

So between the $150 power supply (that you may never get) and the ($300 graphics card off amazon) you are looking at about $450 in an upgrade to basically keep pace with a low level gaming laptop that costs less than what you paid for the HP Envy to begin with.

Which is my biggest problem with this system and the reason for the 3 stars, because it only does what it says (so earns its 3 stars) BUT if it has any sort of hardware issue down the line or doesn't meet your needs, you are going to be stuck buying a whole new system or be left to the mercy of HPs terribly unreliable part store with its over inflated prices and unreliable delivery timetables.
text_fidelity_b: HP ENVY Desktop Computer, Intel Core i7-10700, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB Hard Drive & 512 GB SSD Storage, Windows 10 Pro (TE01-1254, 2020 Model)

Lenovo Legion Y720 Gaming Laptop, 15.6" Full HD, Intel Core i7-7700HQ Processor, 16GB DDR4 RAM, 512GB SSD, GeForce GTX 1060-6GB, Windows 10 Signature Image - 80VR0078US Like all dedicated gaming laptops, this is a big heavy high-powered machine. It is portable enough to lug over to your buddy's house for play dates, but it is too bulky and heavy to carry to work everyday. Construction is very good with an aggressive-looking aluminum case to match the aggressive-sounding "Legion" product name. Mechanical keyboard has decent (but not the best) travel and the large keys are backlit so you can easily play your games in the dark. Dolby Atmos audio works well for games, but is kind of thin for music or movies unless you hook it up to external speakers. This Y720 version has a 1080p IPS display, which is OK but not as bright or contrasty as some other laptops I have used. There is also a more expensive 4K display available, but I have not tried that.

Core i7 CPU with 16GB of RAm gives you really great performance. This machine is easily powerful enough for any games I tried on it. Even though performance is throttled somewhat when run off the battery, battery life is still less than 2 hours under heavy use (maybe 6 hours with light use).

For the money, it is hard to go wrong with these Lenovo Legions. If you don't want to spend more than $1000, the cheaper Legion Y520 is almost as good for most types of games and costs $300 less.
text_fidelity_b: Lenovo Legion Y720 Gaming Laptop, 15.6" Full HD, Intel Core i7-7700HQ Processor, 16GB DDR4 RAM, 512GB SSD, GeForce GTX 1060-6GB, Windows 10 Signature Image - 80VR0078US

text_fidelity_a:
PANASONIC Wings Sport Headphones are Ultra-Light Wireless Bluetooth Sport Earbud 3D Flex Sport Clips with Microphone and Call/Volume Controller, IPX5 Rated Water-Resistant - RP-BTS35-K (Black) I received these earphones from Amazon Vine in early January, 2018. I liked the over-the-ears design. It makes the earphones far less likely to fall off when exercising. The sound quality is also excellent. I found its wireless bluetooth function quite handy for listening to music on my smartphone while walking, biking, lifting weights or doing calisthenics.

In short, as long as the battery could be charged, these sport earphones worked quite well. But suddenly, a few weeks ago, after only 7 months of use, the battery simply would no longer take a charge. The manual says that the battery should last through up to 300 charges, and there is absolutely no way that in only seven months I charged this device 300 times. It holds a charge well while the battery is working, much better than the other bluetooth earbuds that I have owned. So I could use it for up to five days without charging the battery. This means that, in seven months, I only charged the battery about 42-50 times, at most. This means the life of the battery was a mere 16% of what the manufacturer promised!

This is not a device in which the battery can be replaced. Therefore, once the battery dies, the earphones are worthless. Since the warranty is only for 90 days, there is no recourse with the manufacturer for replacing this device after that length of time.

The way that this product works is a good idea, but until the design includes the possibility of replacing the battery, the high price is simply not worth it. I will have to stick to cheap earbuds which are not such a hit to my pocketbook when their non-replaceable battery dies.

I rate this product as follows:

Sound quality 5 stars
Durability of battery: 1 star
Value for price: 1 star
Overall average: 2.3 stars
text_fidelity_b: PANASONIC Wings Sport Headphones are Ultra-Light Wireless Bluetooth Sport Earbud 3D Flex Sport Clips with Microphone and Call/Volume Controller, IPX5 Rated Water-Resistant - RP-BTS35-K (Black)

Wireless Range, Rose Gold These are a nice set of headphones, look-wise. They don't look cheap, fold up well and are fairly comfortable once you get them fitted right. I was getting some ear pain at first, but extended the top a bit and they now fit comfortably.

The bluetooth connected easily and easily allows me to go into the next room and still listen to my iPad that is more centrally located to pick up the wifi. Great for when I'm cleaning and want to listen to podcasts or YouTube. It charged fairly quickly and has lasted about a week of non-continual use. It may not be an issue for someone else, but it caused me to ding it a star. I haven't yet tried these on an airplane, which is where I normally use noise cancelling. But base on how it worked with the A/C, I expect these will do a great job. Just don't expect it to wipe out outside noise. I could still hear the TV going and my husband talking. Just no A/C loud rumbling noise. Now if only I could sleep in these to kill the sound of my husband's fan.

I did get these free in exchange for my honest opinion. What is funny is a just bought a new pair of noise cancelling headphones because my old ones just died and I like these better so far....

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm FinePix Z90 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 5x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens and 3-Inch Touch-Screen LCD (Red) This camera is what I call a "subcompact" - the smallest point and shoot cameras that have vertically mounted lenses which allow protection, compactness, and quicker start up times. Normally, you'd expect a small trade off for these features, so I wouldn't compare this directly with a camera endowed by a telescoping lens.

Sony invented the subcompact with the T1 a few years back (at least in my world), and I was able to compare the FinePix Z90 with the one-generation-older 12 MP Sony T90. I'll go the pro/con route...

PROS of the Z90:

-Price is something like half of the latest subcompact Sony.
-Operational costs are cheaper: USB cable is non-proprietary (in case you want a second one or need to replace it) and SD card is cheaper and more universal than Sony's Memory Stick.
-Separate physical buttons to record movies and to take pictures. This is genius to me, because I hate to miss a great video opportunity while fumbling through the menus.
-Does not come with a memory card, BUT cameras that do usually come with one so small that it is worthless. Internal memory is better, because it allows you to copy from one camera card to another, which can be useful.
-Can set it up to take two photos at once, with and without the flash. As an amateur, I often do this manually anyway, but this way you get closer photos (chronologically)to compare in a dynamic scenario, and the subject needs only to pose once.
-The panorama mode works better than in other cameras I've used. They use internal weights alla smart phones (I'm guessing) to help you line up the next picture. Allows you to "pan" a panorama shot in play mode.
-There is a time zone mode that allows you to temporarily change the time (for timestamps).
-The display changes from horizontal to vertical as you move the camera respectively.
-"Touch and track" mode follows a subject.
-Side by side picture compare.
-Search by face, couple, group, favorites, scene, or date, and view a small picture next to thumbnails.
-Charger is smaller with the plug offset to allow it to use only one receptacle on a power strip (as long as it is at the end of said strip).

CONS of the Z90:

-Picture quality was not as good as the Sony 80% of the time (tested in various modes and lighting conditions). That said, a tripod really helps with low light and no flash, where both cameras struggle without it.
-By numbers, it is not much larger than the Sony, but it feels significantly larger.
-Sometimes the "buttons" in the corners of the touch screen need to be pressed more than once.
-Tripod mount has plastic threads, instead of a machined metal insert.
-Cannot take shots as rapidly as on the Sony
-Does not tell you what zoom level you are at. 5x zoom does not appear to make a great difference over 4x.
-"play" and "camera" buttons could be one button used as a toggle.
-Battery can be put in backward, as the slot is not keyed (although the battery is). No big deal, but shows something wasn't thought out thoroughly.

Bottom Line:

The Fuji is trying to deliver everything the market leader has to offer for a much more manageable price tag. It gets an A for effort, delivering a lot of great menu options, and may actually win in that respect, but the picture quality is not as good. If they could pour a little more money into the actual optics and the touch screen and still keep the price reasonable, they might win the battle in the future. For now, it's purely a personal budget vs. quality decision.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix Z90 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 5x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens and 3-Inch Touch-Screen LCD (Red)

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st) I have an iPhone and PC for all my nerdy electronic gadget needs - why do I need anything else? I really didn't want an electronic device to read from - I'm old fashioned & like carting a paper book around, holding it in one hand folded back, flipping back and forth to re-read pages if I needed. I went kicking & screaming until I realized that I don't have anymore space in the house for my favorite books! So I caved and after some extensive research, I bought a Kindle Fire and a pretty pink leather case from Amazon.com - The options were good and the price was right - and it was in color! I received it in no time flat already programed & ready to start loading it up with books. I was pleasantly surprised with the feel, weight, size and convenience of reading that I explored it's other uses too. I like that fact that I can e-mail docs to my kindle like recipe .pdfs or play games the way I do on my iPhone - Go Angry Birds. I had to wait for HBO Go negotiations for Kindle to complete in June, but now that it's here, I love it - as long as I have internet connection!

Here is what I didn't like so much about it ... maybe something to review for upgrades - next generations...

It's too easy to accidentally press the power button on the bottom end and I can't count how many times I tried to shut down while I was in the middle of something. I lost all my bookmarks to A Song of Ice and Fire once - that was bad.
The power cable connection is very tiny - seems flimsy and also is next to the power button.
And while I have WiFi at home - sometimes I get a weak to no connection (at no fault to the Kindle), it's nice to plug in to the hub to watch movies or surf the Internets.
Oh and I still need to research this, but I like to know page numbers rather than a percentage (is there a setting?)

I can overlook all that - the good out weighs the negative
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st)

text_fidelity_a:
Jiusion Telescope Eyepiece Plossl Eyepiece 32mm with 1.25inch Filter Threaded, Astronomical Telescope Lens 50% FOV increase at this price? This is the lowest priced Plössl I've ever seen and the reason for choosing it. Curiosity.

As a physicist with a too time-consuming career to fool around with optical Garage-a-Tronics projects, it's time for fun. After >40 years, I'd guess 1/3 of my time was in electro-optical systems. My responsibilities included one of the nation's most sophisticated optical design, fabrication, and 50-200 layers of Å thickness vapor deposition coating capability (200 layers is no limit … simply the most I've seen engineered)

You have to give them credit. Chinese optics are extraordinary and have been for 20 years. Asian pricing has wholly changed the marketplace. The crazy low prices have made complex systems affordable to the mass market. Optical grinding facilities remaining in the US are confined to a handful of custom, proto-typing houses run by old-timers with a decidedly different product application than consumer use.

The Plössl eyepiece is quite expensive to manufacture given the nature of the glass, coatings, and its precisely coordinated concave and convex lenses to neutralize internal reflections.

The Plössl has tradeoffs. All optical systems do. For example, Plössl's increased FOV comes with an eye relief confined to 70–80% of focal length.

Lenses are analog. Performance is not binary. 'Lowest price' in optics might be misunderstood. Optics lots begin production targeted at a spec performance that makes a profit. A production lot will yield a normal distribution to spec. On the upper end of the distribution are a few 'blue diamonds' commanding a super premium. Theoretically, 66%, will meet the target spec. Production lots begin life as profitable, spec-centered customers. 7% would be expected to fall short of some spec performance (i.e. start 107% of what you need) … Harvard MBA's demanding perfection in all things except stock value have never come to terms with normal analog distributions in scientific endeavors.

The lenses come without ref to detail specs, so I would believe the factory is emptying the shelves of sub-spec product here. Spec fallout, in my experience, may have little or nothing to do with operator perceptions of performance.

Excellent fun.

Was my review helpful? If so, click "Helpful" so I can know. Trying hard to put integrity into reviews
text_fidelity_b: Jiusion Telescope Eyepiece Plossl Eyepiece 32mm with 1.25inch Filter Threaded, Astronomical Telescope Lens

text_fidelity_a:
Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) This is a good tablet for the price, but it is really crippled by the lack of support for the Google Play store. I have purchased many apps for my Android smartphone that I cannot run on this tablet because they are not available in the Amazon store. Others are available on Amazon, but I would have to pay for them again to run them on this tablet (I could download them without additional cost on other Android tablets that support the Google Play store). Support for the Amazon Prime cloud services is great, though not much different from what you would get on other Android tablets.

If you mostly run free apps, then this tablet is worth considering. If you would have to re-buy a lot of apps that you have already purchased for other Android devices, then this tablet may not make financial sense for you. Other Android tablets cost more, but can give you a much brighter and sharper screen and faster performance.

Yes, some people are hacking the Amazon Fire tablet to add Google Play support, but the process is somewhat time consuming and complicated. If you're smart enough to do that, in the time it takes you to perform this hack, you could easily earn enough money to buy a better tablet in the first place.

text_fidelity_a:
Outdoor WiFi Security Camera, HD 1080P Wireless Survenience IP Camera with 32GB SD Card, IP66 Waterproof Bullet Camera for Home, Support Motion Detection FTP 65ft Night Vision Remote View Onvif Cam [[VIDEOID:bcc01f35bd32d1e66d3df81c3dace063]] Updated as promised: After working with the company I was able to completely secure the camera and still access it remotely. After all the initial problems and concerns I have had it installed and working for about a month I guess. It's working great on a variety of different software and protocols. I even tried connecting it to the Angelcam website and using DDNS. Works great with just about everything. With the 128GB SD card it does great. I uploaded some new photos of it working and the different clients being used securely. This turned out to be a great buy because the image quality is incredible and it's got an incredibly wide angle.

You cannot see the IR light like that at night it's only because of the camera I used you can see it. I did that for a reason so that everyone could see the amount of IR light it puts out. The infrared works great as you can see but the motion sensor even on the least sensitive setting picks up rains and bugs flying in front of it. Almost all motion sensors do. The audio sensor works great but the alarm feature doesn't because it's only one way audio. The email was easy to setup once you know which smtp server your ISP uses which WOW doesn't like giving theirs out even to paying customers. The video was provided by them and helped a lot because the screws were impossible to see and there are unnecessary ones in there that don't need to be removed. I have posted the material they sent me as well. I hope this helps everyone out.

BEFORE EDIT AND CUSTOMER SUPPORT:
So far I have had a lot of issues with this camera and still haven't got it to where I would trust letting it outside my isolated LAN which mean I cannot view remotely as of yet. I changed the 32Gb SD card out to a 128Gb card after contacting support since there is no instructions online or anywhere else on how to do it. Turns out it's the one tiny screw in on the top to remove the black piece and then you must carefully unscrew the lens cap. After that you will find several screws lowered besides the lens and IR area. You only need to remove the 4 of the screws. If you look really close with magnification you can see exactly what screws you need to remove because you can see how they hold the board underneath in place. Underneath the lens is the board that holds the SD-Card. Their support was nice enough to send me a video later on. I plan on posting that later after I get this all working. As of now it is telling me I need to reset the camera and there is no reset button that I can find. I am guessing it must be on that board again which means I am going to have to pull the whole thing apart again. In my opinion this is very poorly designed and not very good for people who like to customize or configure their devices. I do not like the way the it acts as soon as it connects to your network. I am still working on testing and hope I can get these issues resolved soon. The picture quality is great but there is a serious lack of security and other major issues plaguing this device. I am going to do some further testing and contact support once again about resetting this camera hopefully without having to dissemble it again but I don't see how. It has been disconnected for hours without power and will not reset that way. I also notice that the camera unit get's extremely hot for some reason. This will defiantly shorten it's life span. More to come on this product but for now I do not recommend buying this unless you are familiar with IP camera installation, network configuration, and have some electrical experience as far as handling circuit boards. This has been a real pain in the read since day one but I am hoping it will be worth it but time will tell. I will upload the video provided by them after getting their consent.
text_fidelity_b: Outdoor WiFi Security Camera, HD 1080P Wireless Survenience IP Camera with 32GB SD Card, IP66 Waterproof Bullet Camera for Home, Support Motion Detection FTP 65ft Night Vision Remote View Onvif Cam

text_fidelity_a:
Click 'n Dig Model E4 Key Finder. 4 Receivers. Wireless RF Remote Item, Wallet Locator Okay, this is an update to the one-star review I emitted originally. The Click 'n' Dig folks are definitely getting their money's worth from their PR people, whom I would hire myself if I could afford to hire someone who works that hard. After viewing my crabby review (below), they got in touch and offered to send a new set (you get the key finder and several other pieces that you can attach to other easily lost items). Surely, said they, the set shipped to me must have been defective. Would I take another one and if it improved, would I consider re-reviewing?

Oh, why not? I have nothing else to do during the hours left around the seven 14-hour days a week entailed in running a business. :-D They sent the doodads in the mail.

MEANWHILE... Between the time I first posted my original grutch and the time the new package of goodies arrived, I lost my keys not once, not twice, but THREE TIMES.

Each time, the Key Finder located the things! Inside a purse...on a piece of furniture where I'd dropped the keys to rescue the dog...atop a countertop where no one in their right mind would ever leave their keys...

It's not a matter of standing wherever you happen to be and clicking the "finder" device. You do have to walk around the house, and you do have to point the finder in several directions until it locates and connects with the receiver on your keyring. Its signal will pass through some but not all walls (why, I do not know: possibly electrical wiring or insulation?). Its range is about 20 feet, I'd guess. It requires some patience and persistence on your part, but it does eventually work.

Click 'n' Dig sent me a new set, which I gave to some dear friends who are even more superannuated than I after the Missus expressed dismay at having lost her keys once again. This is one of those tools that makes old age tolerable...maybe even survivable.

***********

ORIGINAL WHINGE: Not sending this back, because I don't have time to hassle with repackaging and mailing. But can't recommend it. These devices are supposed to emit a 90-decibel beep when you point the hand-held radio transmitter at them. Thus if you have one on, say, a key ring, you should be able to locate the keys if you misplace them around the house. We're told the radio frequency goes through walls and has an 80-foot range.

Well, if that's 90 decibels, then 90 decibels isn't very loud. According to Purdue University, 90 db is as loud as a "Boeing 737 or DC-9 aircraft at one nautical mile (6080 ft) before landing (97 dB); power mower (96 dB); motorcycle at 25 ft (90 dB). Newspaper press (97 dB)." Dang! I wish!! If aircraft made the same level of sound as this handy-dandy beeper, the skies would be a lot quieter around here!! :-D And my neighbor's Harley would be a lot more fun, too...

No, the signal does not go through walls.

The range is about 25 feet. Any further away than that, and the transmitter will not elicit a beep. If your keys have dropped out of your pocket and slipped under a chair cushion, you have to be right on top of the chair to get receiver to beep.

Could be the gadgets need new batteries, which are kindly included. But the instructions do not show how to find the battery cases or how to open them. On the key fob, it's obvious enough where the battery case is, but you can't get it open -- I split a fingernail and hurt my finger when I tried. On the flat gadgets that you can stick to objects with the provided double-sided tape, I can't even find a CLUE to where a battery case could be opened. ?????????

The idea behind this device is truly brilliant. Sure do wish the execution were better.
text_fidelity_b: Click 'n Dig Model E4 Key Finder. 4 Receivers. Wireless RF Remote Item, Wallet Locator

text_fidelity_a:
Fitbit Versa Smart Watch, Peach/Rose Gold Aluminium, One Size (S & L Bands Included), Heart Rate Monitor This little device does a lot.
While it is sort of a smart watch, it sort of isn't, too. But what it does, it does well.

The good:
- Excellent selection of watch faces, including cute, clever, big, pretty, etc. You can change your face every day to match your clothes if you want.
- If I understand correctly, you can use it with other services, like Spark People.
- measures pulse, steps, miles. Tracks exercise on demand.
- motivates in numerous ways. Reminders to stand up, encouragement to finish your goal steps for the hour, challenges, even "travel" challenges that are longer term.
- large userbase. You can network with more of your friends on Fitbit than on any other fitness watch.
- big face without losing attractiveness
- large variety of replacement bands available from third parties, some very pretty.
- Can be used with many other fitness applications.
- Detects sleep surprisingly accurately
- Lots of settings options
- A decent number of apps available
- Handles the shower well
- If you never have to take it off except to charge, it's harder to lose it.
- Charges very quickly
- The charger is an awesome design and easy to use
- You can always have your alarms with you so you never miss them.

The irritating
- All changes have to be made through the app.
- If you don't sync often enough, it loses your data
- Sync can take a long time.
- The battery life is considerably shorter than I expected. It's about 2 1/2 days if I have constant sync turned off.
- Don't even bother with constant sync unless you're willing to take it off to charge a lot.
- All the music apps are paid

All in all, though, the pros are big and the cons are small. Enough that it still warrants a 5 star review.

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Chromebook (Wi-Fi, 11.6-Inch) 2012 Model I am director of a small publishing house. I've been using a $1,000 MacBook Pro 11.6 (Lion) laptop for over a year, with the Chrome browser, Gmail, and GoogleDrive as my online backup for laptop-based files of importance. I got accustomed to the trackpad (I switched the scrolling direction) and haven't used a mouse since I got my Mac. I do book production and cover design on it, sitting in the living room recliner (too far from an electrical outlet to use the adapter) but the battery runs down pretty quickly.

I wanted this Chromebook as a second machine for starting and ending my day: browsing and doing the cloud-based work I have to do, like accounting in Wave, managing social network-based marketing, ordering books, searching for cover art, reading manuscripts in Submittable, handling email, etc. My Mac with Adobe CS5 is essential for the actual book design and production, so I basically reserve its battery now for that.

What is amazing to me is how similar this Chromebook keyboard is to my MacBook Pro. The only time I realize I'm not on my Mac is when I hit what, on the Mac, is the caps lock key but on the Chromebook pops up apps. (There is no caps lock key on the Chromebook; supposedly you can press both shift keys at the same time to effect caps lock, but I guess I don't have the right touch because I can't get it to work.) Another slight difference is in how click and drag works; on the Chromebook, you hit the trackpad with your thumb, then drag.

Those who have already gotten accustomed to using Google-related commands for email, clearing the cache, and the like will be good to go without any learning curve. Chrome extensions and apps, of course, work as expected. (I am SO glad I had the prescience to realize a year ago that I definitely wanted to shift to a cloud-based approach!)

Now, a word about the quality of the monitor. I find the type on the screen to be MORE readable than on my Mac. It is much crisper and high-definition. The colors don't match between the two computers, but I'm not sure it's the Chromebook's fault. The Chromebook does seem to be able to sense how to adjust brightness based on the conditions of the room, which is helpful. Sometimes, however, my eyes start smarting, something that happens when I'm working on the Chromebook, but not on the MacBook Pro. I don't know what accounts for this. The sound is better on the Chromebook than on my Mac, especially if I use good headphones. When watching a movie, the color is a bit washed out compared to the really garishly brightly colored sets, but I prefer that.

I'm probably more of a power user when it comes to the user end of a computer, but I don't try to get in and hack things like some people do. Developer mode, need for static IP address, etc., I'm clueless about. But this is a well-built, fast, mostly no-fuss, low-cost and very light-weight piece of work with a long-lasting battery, which is exactly what I wanted. That I also got a seamless experience shifting from one machine to the other for a quarter of what my MacBook Pro cost? That's priceless!
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Chromebook (Wi-Fi, 11.6-Inch) 2012 Model
